research_text:
## 1. Governed API and meaning of the reported value

`javax.crypto.spec.IvParameterSpec` is an `AlgorithmParameterSpec` that holds an initialization vector (IV). Its two constructors accept either an entire byte array or a selected array range; the class copies the supplied bytes, and `getIV()` returns a new array. The API itself documents no requirement that the bytes come from a random source. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/IvParameterSpec.html))

The reported wording—“no randomized source of the iv given to `IvParameterSpec(byte[])` was observed”—therefore refers to the `byte[] iv` argument supplied when constructing an `IvParameterSpec` with the one-argument constructor. It is **not** a Java runtime exception or a condition documented by the `IvParameterSpec` API. It corresponds to the CrySL rule’s required provenance predicate, `randomized[iv]`; the rule text does not define which generators, transformations, or interprocedural paths establish that predicate. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/IvParameterSpec.crysl))

Oracle’s general JCA guidance distinguishes the broader cryptographic context from this holder class:

- In its discussion of simple block-cipher modes, Oracle states that an IV “should be random” and need not be secret. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html))
- `IvParameterSpec` itself does not specify an IV length, uniqueness/reuse requirement, or any mode-specific rule. It only defines byte-array construction and range/null checks. The appropriate requirements therefore depend on the selected cipher transformation and provider. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/IvParameterSpec.html))
- GCM is not fully parameterized by `IvParameterSpec`: the Java API documents `GCMParameterSpec` as carrying both an IV and an authentication-tag length. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/GCMParameterSpec.html))

## 2. Officially documented safe usage and remediation boundaries

### What the official Java sources document

For encryption where a cipher requires parameters such as an IV, the JCA Reference Guide says that if no parameters are supplied to `Cipher.init`, the provider is supposed to supply required parameters, either by generating random parameters or by using provider-specific defaults. The resulting IV or parameter object can be retrieved through `Cipher.getIV()` or `Cipher.getParameters()`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html))

Where an application supplies IV bytes itself, Java’s `SecureRandom` API is the standard JCA random-byte facility: it provides a cryptographically strong RNG and exposes `nextBytes` for retrieving random bytes. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/SecureRandom.html))

For decryption, the JCA guide says that **the same parameters used for encryption must be used for decryption**. It further documents recovering stored encoded algorithm parameters via `AlgorithmParameters` before initializing the decrypting cipher. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html))

### What the sources do *not* document

There is no official `IvParameterSpec` documentation that:

- defines “randomized” as a provenance property;
- tells users to replace every supplied IV with a newly generated one;
- supplies a generic one-size-fits-all IV length;
- defines a general remediation procedure for a non-random IV; or
- says that an IV received or recovered for decryption should be regenerated.

Accordingly, the documented direction is conditional: Oracle’s general guidance says random IVs should be used in its simple block-cipher encryption discussion, while the decryption guidance requires using the original encryption parameters. The supplied CrySL file has no declared event for cipher operation mode, cipher transformation, encryption/decryption state, storage, or message parsing, so the rule text alone cannot resolve which documented case applies. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html))

## 3. Compatibility, persisted data, wire formats, and migration

### API/platform compatibility

`IvParameterSpec` has been part of Java since version **1.4**. The current Java SE API still declares the same two constructors:

- `IvParameterSpec(byte[] iv)`
- `IvParameterSpec(byte[] iv, int offset, int len)` ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/IvParameterSpec.html))

### Persisted and wire formats

The `IvParameterSpec` API documents an in-memory parameter object and byte-array copying. It does **not** define:

- a serialized representation for `IvParameterSpec`;
- a wire format containing an IV;
- an envelope format combining ciphertext, IV, tag, algorithm identifier, or version; or
- a migration format/version marker. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/IvParameterSpec.html))

At the `Cipher`/JCA level, Oracle documents that encryption parameters may be obtained as `AlgorithmParameters`; their encoded form can be stored and later used to initialize decryption. Oracle also states that the same parameters used for encryption must be used for decryption. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html))

### Documented migration path

No official Java source located specifies a migration path for changing IV-generation behavior in already persisted ciphertext or protocol records. The only documented compatibility requirement relevant to existing encrypted data is preservation and reuse of the encryption parameters for decryption. Therefore, the sources do not support assuming that previously stored ciphertext can be decrypted with a newly generated IV. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html))

## 4. Exact CrySL rule match and conditions

The supplied source declares one governed specification type: `javax.crypto.spec.IvParameterSpec`. Its matching declaration is:

```text
SPEC javax.crypto.spec.IvParameterSpec

OBJECTS
	byte[] iv;
	int offset;
	int len;

EVENTS
	c1: IvParameterSpec(iv);
	c2: IvParameterSpec(iv, offset, len);
	Con := c1 | c2;
```

([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/IvParameterSpec.crysl))

**Match scope stated by that source:**

- **Receiver/governed type:** `javax.crypto.spec.IvParameterSpec`.
- **Matched member forms:** constructor events named `IvParameterSpec`, not ordinary instance or static methods.
- **Parameter-list match:** exactly one byte-array variable, `iv`, for `c1`; or exactly `iv, offset, len` for `c2`.
- **Alternative event:** `Con := c1 | c2` means either declared constructor event is accepted by the declared order. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/IvParameterSpec.crysl))

The source then declares these conditions:

```text
CONSTRAINTS
	length[iv] >= offset + len;
	offset >= 0;
	len > 0;

REQUIRES
	randomized[iv];

ENSURES
	preparedIV[this];
```

([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/IvParameterSpec.crysl))

Thus, for either declared constructor event, the rule requires `randomized[iv]` and ensures `preparedIV[this]`. It also declares the three listed `CONSTRAINTS`.

**Can it match a method merely because it shares a name with the governed API? No, not from this rule text.** The sole declared specification target is the fully qualified type `javax.crypto.spec.IvParameterSpec`, and the sole events are the two constructor-shaped declarations above. The source contains no wildcard, alternate receiver type, or ordinary method declaration that would extend matching to a method on an unrelated type with the same spelling. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/IvParameterSpec.crysl))

## Source limitations and unresolved questions

- The CrySL source does not define the analyzer semantics of `randomized[iv]`, including recognized random sources, propagation through helpers, decoding/copying behavior, or whether the predicate applies to all bytes or a selected range.
- For event `c1`, only `iv` is bound, while the rule-wide constraints also reference `offset` and `len`; the source does not explain how those variables are interpreted for the one-argument constructor.
- The rule has no cipher-use event and does not state whether the constructed IV is used for encryption, decryption, GCM, a feedback mode, or anything else.
- The Java documentation provides general and API-level semantics, but does not define an application’s persisted ciphertext or protocol format.
